text: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to Yageo's third quarter results webcast. I'm Howard Kao, the analyst covering Yageo at Morgan Stanley, and I'll be moderating today's discussion. Yageo is the world's largest supplier of chip resistors and tantalum capacitors, and a top-three global supplier of MLCCs and inductors. Joining us from Yageo today are David Wang, President and CEO; Eddie Chen and Claudio Lollini, co-COOs; and Gaven Dong, CFO. Thank you all for being with us.

Gaven will begin by walking us through the third quarter results, followed by David's remarks on the business outlook. We'll then open the discussion to questions from the audience. You may submit your questions at any time during the webcast using the text box on your screen. And with that, I'll turn the call over to Gaven. Gaven, please go ahead.

Thank you, Howard. Everyone, welcome to our Q3 earnings call. If you could move to the next slide, please. So I will start by sharing our Q3 financial results. We had a very successful quarter on both the top line and the bottom line. If you look at our revenue in Q3, we generated 49.5 billion dollars. Not only is this a record high, but also this is the seventh consecutive quarter we delivered better quarterly revenue than the previous quarter.

If you look at the numbers on the left, you will see 49.5 billion dollars of revenue, 11.4% higher than the previous quarter, almost 50% higher than the same period of last year. This is largely due to AI-driven demand. At the same time, I think we would like to highlight we see growth quarter-on-quarter across all product lines, customer segments, and regions, which I will cover the details later.

On the profitability side, you see gross margin ratio is 41% in Q3, 2.5 percentage points better than the previous quarter, and almost 5 percentage points better than the same period of last year. In the dollar terms, gross profit is actually 19% higher than last quarter and 70% higher than the same period of last year. On the operating margin side, 29.5%, 3.1 percentage points better than last quarter and 6.6% better than the same period of last year. EBITDA margin also very strong, almost 35%, 2.4 percentage points better than last quarter and almost 5 percentage points better than the same period of last year. Very strong cash generation capability from us.

On the net income dollar, as I mentioned, very strong top line and higher profitability result as higher net income dollar as well. We generated 12 billion dollars net income dollar, 27.2% higher than previous quarter, and almost 89% higher than same period of last year. EPS from Q3 is 5.83 dollars per share, similar result compared with previous quarter and also same period of last year. On the revenue side, as already mentioned, AI continued driving the demand, but again, we see strong demand from customer across the board. On the profitability side, largely due to favorable product mix, price adjustment, and also higher efficiencies. With that, let's move on to the year-to-date results.

So from the first nine months, we generated 132 billion dollars of revenue, 36% higher than same period of last year. Gross margin percentage point is 39.3%, approaching 40%, 3.5 percentage points better than same period of last year. Operating margin 27.2%, 5.5 percentage points better than first nine months in last year. EBITDA margin 33.1%, 4.4 percentage points better than last year. Similar result as I mentioned for Q3, year-to-date net income dollar is 29.4 billion dollars, 74% better than same period of last year. Similar result you can see from EPS. From the first nine months, we generated 14.3 dollars per share, 74% better than last year.

I will give you some details on the revenue breakdown by product and by segment. On the top chart, you can see our revenue breakdown by product line. A few things I'd like to highlight. If you look at the MLCC, which is the dark blue bar, the share of the total revenue has increased from 19.1% to 21.5%. I will also remind you this is based on much higher revenue base, right? As I just mentioned, Q3 revenue is 11.4% higher than Q2. So both a higher base and a higher share show strong demand in MLCC. This is really the result of AI-related customer demand.

Speaking of AI, we're also happy to report AI has contributed almost 20% of our total revenue. You can also see that from the bottom chart. In the Computing & Enterprise, share has increased from 27.3% to 28.3%. This is against the backdrop of softening demand from laptop and PC. So this is clear demonstration of the strong demand from AI. At the same time, I would highlight across all segments we see in absolute dollar terms quarter-on-quarter growth. Next slide, please.

Here we would like to show the revenue breakdown by region and by channels. Again, very healthy, very structured and balanced revenue source. This is really one of our strengths in Yageo. One thing I'd like to highlight is if you look at distributors, we have been seeing steadily decreasing inventory level, which is really a strong demonstration of the demand from the end customers.

You can see our free cash flow in Q3 much higher than the previous three quarters. Although we actually had a higher CapEx in this quarter, this is really the result of strong top line, very good profitability, and we have been continue managing our operating working capital. On the bottom chart, you see our net debt against our EBITDA, very strong, very healthy. This is really a solid springboard of our future expansion. With that, I'll pass on to David to share the outlook for Q4.

Thank you, Gaven. So for Q4 outlook, usually Q4 the last quarter of the year is the low season of the year. So in the past, we could give the guidance like lower than Q3, or sometimes as flat as Q3. But this year, because we still see very strong demand and we also see very strong B/B ratio, especially the B/B ratio of special product rather than the commodity product. So although this is low season, so we give the net sales guidance is slightly increase quarter on quarter. And consequently, because of the higher volume, also better product mix, we also see the gross margin and the operating income will be slightly higher than Q3. So this is the guidance we like to pass to the to the audience. Thank you, Howard.

Thank you, Gaven and David, for walking us through the results and outlook. We'll now move on to the Q&A session. As a reminder, please submit your questions using the text box on your screen. And to get us started, I'd like to talk about first on the third quarter results. Gaven, you mentioned earlier that there was some impact on margins driven by higher costs. Can you talk a little bit more about that? What was the higher input cost, and is there any way to offset it and mitigate those higher costs going forward?

Yeah, sure, happy to. Well, actually you can see our results, right? Gross margin has been increasing quarter-over-quarter. This is really the efforts from, you know, managing our input cost actively. So we're doing a lot of things, including better efficiencies, pooling our purchase behavior, and also finding second and third sourcing source, right? At the same time, on the top line, we're also adjusting our price accordingly, not only the input cost, but also the supply and demand. I think the result tells itself, right? We see the result from all this effort continue improving our gross margin. I hope that answers the question.

Yeah, yeah, perfect. And some housekeeping questions here to start with. First, on utilization rate. Can you walk us through what was the utilization rate for standard and specialty in Q3, and what is your expectation for this quarter?

In Q3, both specialty and commodity, they are very close to 95%. Now because of the strong demand, we see Q4 this will be higher than 95%. We know this is very tight, but at the same time, we also do efficiency improvement, also do some debottleneck, also increase the capacity gradually. Hopefully this can support the very strong demand in the coming quarters. So both utilization, commodity and specialty, in Q4 will be higher than 95%.

I see. Thank you, David. Just a follow-up on this, as we look into 2027, and I think market expectation as well as our expectation is demand for AI will continue to be extremely strong. Will capacity be a concern to think about when we model out your revenues over the next couple of quarters?

Well, actually in the beginning of this year, we do plan to increase our capacity. So gradually we see the capacity will be increased quarter-on-quarter. Also again, some debottleneck and also the efficiency improvement. So we do hope that because of all these efforts, we can support the strong demand in the coming quarter, you know, or in 2027.

I see. Thank you. And does your current order book support a healthy start to 2027? I think typically, as you mentioned in your prepared remarks, Q4 is flat or slightly down quarter-on-quarter, but you see an uptick in Q1. Now you have a higher base in the fourth quarter. Does that also mean Q1 will continue to grow, or will there be a change in seasonality for the first quarter of next year?

I can answer you by our B/B ratio. We see still in Q3, the B/B ratio is almost 2. And don't forget, in Q3 we have higher revenue than Q2. So based on that higher basis, we still see very strong B/B ratio, especially in AI-related products, such as tantalum capacitor or MLCC, very, very high book-to-bill ratio.
I see. So just to clarify, two, sorry, almost two, is that on a blended basis? So when you said tantalum and MLCC is even stronger, these two segments will be higher than two?
Two is the company average, so it's blended. So which means the other strong product can be higher than that.

And on inventory, can I ask about inventory for both your direct customers as well as for distributors? Is this something that you've seen change materially in the past couple of months, or is it still sitting at a relatively healthy level? And roughly how many months or weeks of inventory would that be?

Howard, I'll give you some comments on the inventory sitting in the channel, which it's a good proxy on the customer side. And Yageo does have a significant percentage of revenue through the channel. As always, we split the channel between Greater China and more like global distributors. Global distributors' months on hand over the last three months reduced from about 5 months now to 4. And for the Greater China distribution piece, over the last three months, the months on hand was already very tight, very low, and it remained below 2.

So in both cases, because they run with different business model, the inventory is low. And in fact, the channel, both sides of the channel is an active driver for growth as they try to get ahead of demand and restock and make sure they do have inventory.

Got it. Thank you. So it sounds like inventory or a buildup of inventory is not a concern that we should think about over the next couple of months. But when we look at the consumer segment, seems like demand is getting weaker and weaker and declining quite sharply. Is this something that concerns you guys?

For what we classify as consumer, we're still growing quarter-over-quarter and year-over-year in dollar terms. And I advise to look at this perhaps in dollar terms, because when you look at the percentage of the business, as long as you have AI kind of driving and pushing computing so much, it may be misleading. But in dollar terms, consumer year-over-year still grow about 20% for us in dollar terms. It's just that it's not keeping up with the pace of the growth in other segments like industrial, which is more than 40, or computing, enterprise and telecom, which is more than 50% in dollar terms year-over-year.

Got it. And just maybe to kind of dig into this a little bit more, would you say over the past three months, you know, since we last spoke on the second quarter earnings call, within your computing segment, I know you said remains strong, but has demand changed materially in the past three months based on your conversations with customers?

We continue to see, like Gaven alluded to in his opening, the laptop and notebook segment to be not particularly strong. Smartphone are doing a little better than than before. The overall consumer is not as strong as the other segments, but it's for us, as I said, continues to grow. Not really a significant change in the demand that we see. We continue to see growth in industrial EMEA, which is great. It's now like seven consecutive quarters of growth in dollar-based. We continue to see automotive being a segment that has growth mostly out of Asia, but still struggling in the traditionally Tier 1 European-based companies. And overall, we continue to see the growth in computing, enterprise, telecom is a very associated segment to it, and the overarching defense and aerospace, although from a low base. No significant change, Howard. I think we are closing the year with the same pattern that we saw leading up to to this point.

Got it. Got it. And just transitioning to pricing, I know this is what investors care a lot about, maybe something that you guys don't want to talk too much about, but from a pricing perspective, especially for MLCCs, can you kind of help us compare for some of these more standard products that you're selling now and that you sold maybe during the 2018 upcycle? Kind of where we are in terms of pricing compared to that last upcycle? Are there any comparisons that you can share with us? Are we 50% there, 40%, just any color that you can share with us?

Maybe I'll start by addressing some of the differences between the two cycles that I see and observe. At that time, especially for Yageo, and if you recall, at that time, Yageo was a very different company. Yageo didn't have yet executed all the major acquisitions that really transformed the organization. So it was purely an MLCC and chip resistor component manufacturer. The exposure also to the market was at that time very heavy on Greater China, very heavy on local distribution. And also within the MLCC, it didn't have the portfolio that KEMET added, so it didn't have a lot of the specialty part. It didn't have the automotive exposure, and certainly it didn't have the same type of exposure in global distribution.

Having said that, at that time, the cycle was very fast, very violent, in a way, driven by not any sector in particular, if not consumer, or just a broader impact. And the major root cause at the end of it was really the unwillingness of several players to invest enough in CapEx given the returns that they were getting at that time over the long period of time, over like 10 years. The MLCC demand in the previous 10 years doubled in quantity, but extracted the same dollars. This kind of hit at the same time, and the MLCC shortage created a frenziness in a demand. There were cases of customers bidding to be able to have a supplier shifting capacity to them. So pricing at that time was not very sustainable over the longer period of time, I feel.

This time, the pricing structure and the conversations that we have around customers, not just on MLCC, but all products, feels much more resilient, structured, organized. The framework with which we are operating is now driven by demand, is now driven by an AI push for more computing power, more efficiencies, which kind of lead to more volume, more specialties, higher capacitance, density, and everything that comes with it. And yes, it is playing in computing and telecom, but is now making inroads in industrial and other segments. So overall, I feel suppliers are more prepared, CapEx has been deployed better, and we don't see that same frenziness when it came to pricing. So if you compare pricing point, it might be lower now compared to the peaks that we have in 2018, but more sustainable, and I feel much more appropriate for what supply and demand balance really is.

Got it. Thank you. That was very helpful. But just to stick on pricing, I think there are a couple of your competitors that I think raised prices in the fourth quarter. How do you think about pricing going to next year? You mentioned you guys have capacity coming online, your competitors have capacity coming online. Will pricing continue to move upwards, or do you think we are already at an elevated level, and through 2027 pricing will just remain stable?

Great question, by the way. As we model next year, you know, we ask ourselves the same. And ultimately, the answer always lies on the market, the supply and demand. And we can try to model a lot of different scenarios, but only as you go through it, you will see what that demand and supply balance or lack of will do on pricing, with the additional element of the cost structure. Now for the cost structure, we feel that we have taken the necessary steps and we feel that it was well communicated to customers. As for the demand and supply for next year, at the moment, the proxy we can give is our book-to-bill ratio, like David said. And we know that the market is dynamic and very fluid and it may change, but we are clearly closing the year with momentum and entering next year with momentum. So we will need to see, Howard, and have a discussion with customers and distributors then based on what we see.

Got it. Got it. And in terms of just, you know, sticking to MLCC, in terms of the recent announcement between TDK and Taiyo Yuden and their MOU, can you share your thoughts on how you guys view that partnership, how that impacts the industry, whether if it's good or bad, and why?
We can only judge based on what was shared publicly. So we saw it, we read it. I don't think it's changing anything in our in our direction. We don't really have a lot to comment on on this.

Got it. And on AI server-related MLCCs, as you mentioned, demand is strong. I think Semco at their earnings call yesterday also mentioned that demand is extremely strong and they're expecting demand to grow 8x for them, I think for specific high-end MLCCs. Do you see that tightening the supply of the standard segment for your products?

We believe that overall for us, the major revenue growth contribution still is specialty-related product. So they're both growing, but as David said, also in the book-to-bill, we still see the specialty being more a bigger contributor. Having said that, the commodity piece is doing well. Do we have some spillover effect from those other players that kind of shift more broadly towards the specialty, leaving perhaps unattended the commodity market? Probably, maybe. But quite frankly, it's very hard for us to really go and try to measure that and track this. It's really just a supposition for now. It's possible.

I see. So in your conversations with your customers, have they said to you that, you know, they're shifting more over because they are not getting enough capacity elsewhere? Is that something that you're hearing from your customers?

Typically, they don't really tell us what's going on with their other suppliers. It's an information they rather not share. They may simply ask for more capacity or more support based on overall needs going up or making different decisions. We're seldomly aware of really what is the motive behind. So again, you would need to ask them, really.

I see. All right. Thank you. And can I just come back to ask a little bit about the BB ratio? David, you mentioned BB ratio is now close to 2. If I recall correctly, I think last quarter it was a little bit above 2. So can you kind of talk about what changed, and do you think this will continue to decline or will it inflect upwards in the next couple of months?

Well, as said, we don't see the booking decline. Because the BB ratio is based on the billing. Now if you see the Q3 billing is 11% higher than Q2, so with that strong base, we still see the very strong booking. The mathematics, then the BB ratio could be a little bit lower than last quarter, but actually booking still strong.

Got it. Thank you for that clarification. And I want to touch a little bit about LTAs. I think in the last earnings call, it was mentioned that customers are engaging with you guys on LTAs. So over the past three months, how much of that has been converted into actual signed agreements? Because again, I think your competitor Semco mentioned that they have signed a lot of LTAs with around 50 customers, and their LTAs covered more than 50% of their revenues for next year. So I want to ask how many of that conversations the past three months have actually been converted into actual signed LTAs?

We certainly have had active conversation and I would say notable notable agreements with a couple of large customers. We haven't publicly came out and provided too many details of that, and just a different communication strategy, I guess, compared to other suppliers. So we'd like to continue down that philosophy. Having said that, we also see the number of conversations regarding supply with our customers being now the predominant theme. And when we look at customers trying to secure their supply for next year, we also see that the backlog, which means the firm orders we have on hand, continue to grow year-over-year, quarter-over-quarter, month-over-month. So that to me is essentially a contract. That to me is essentially a commitment from a customer to place orders to secure the supply and the production. And for most, if not all of our major customers, we have contract in place already and the negotiations or the conversations around supply and demand just follow the same pattern, especially now being year-end. So I would say very similar theme and momentum as you described, but we're just not sharing all the details about what has been agreed or not, or signed or not.

Right, it sounds like it's fair to assume or say that things are moving positively, more customers are engaging with you guys, maybe not just on MLCC, but across all other product segments, and seems like interest is getting higher and higher.

Yeah, and certain customers that see growth, like significant growth, they also come to us because they know they can source, I wouldn't say all passives, but they can definitely source majority of their bill of material when it comes to passives, like capacitors, for instance. We are one of the very few, if not the only company, that can give you an MLCC, a tantalum, a film, aluminum electrolytic capacitor, a chip, of course. We are the largest provider in the world. But also we can add to it magnetics. We can add magnetics from inductors all the way to large transformers, chokes, and now sensors on top. So many customers come to us because they try to reduce the number of conversations and the number of unknown and surprises they can have with suppliers for all of these passive components and passive-related, I should say. So when we have those conversations, Howard, it is rarely only about MLCC. Of course, MLCC might be the one that triggered the conversation, but it's never the only product that gets to talk about and that we ultimately agree to supply.
Got it. Got it. And just coming back to your Q4 outlook, there's a question here asking how should we think about that slight quarter-on-quarter revenue increase between ASP and volume?
Both will play a role, just like Q3. We look into it, we try to estimate it. Both were relevant in Q3, and we believe both will be relevant in Q4, too.

Thank you. And on your AI revenue mix, I think, Gaven, it was you that mentioned that revenue reached 20% in Q3. If I recall correctly, it was around 16% in the second quarter. That kind of 4% difference, was that mainly driven by MLCC, as you mentioned, you know, going from 19% of our revenues in the last quarter to 21% this quarter?

Howard, allow me to give some color on this, too. Yeah, it was 16% in Q2, it was 15% in Q1, and at some point last year was like 5%, so it's been a tremendous story. Q-on-Q, it was MLCC, but not only. For us, AI is definitely heavy on capacitors, so MLCC, but don't forget tantalum, very much utilized in Computing & Telecom, which are the primary exposure for AI. But now also film, and in particular aluminum electrolytic, having a lot of adoption in AI, an AI-related application, especially on the power side. And so really, not to mention resistors, which is across the board. Inductors plays a role. So if you want to single out MLCC, maybe, but I would say all capacitors really are supporting that growth in percentage. And that growth in percentage is really driven by that momentum and growth of customers, but also an expansion of the AI penetration that we observe in the same segment, but also now into less traditionally AI segments like industrial, for instance. I think very soon AI will be very embedded in all of them, just like AI will be very embedded in the workspace. So it will become more and more difficult to really segment and carve out AI revenue, because all of it will be somewhat driven by AI.
Got it. Thank you. And on capacity expansion, there are a few questions here asking if you can share any color on how much capacity you intend to expand for 2027?
We do have a plan for both tantalum and MLCC. Well, I cannot disclose the number here, but basically we are talking about maybe 10 to 15% increase quarter-on-quarter...
10 to... sorry, first of all, thank you, David. So to clarify...
So to clarify, not 10 to 15% increase quarter each quarter. So now we are looking now maybe to increase 10 to 15% higher than the current capacity.
I see. Got it, got it. Very clear. And is there a timeline as to when that capacity is expected to come online? Is that Q1 next year, or is it like second half next year?
Some of them will be realized in Q2, and some of them will be in the second half of the year. We plan this schedule very carefully in order to meet all the demand.

I see. So is it fair to say that your strategy is to expand enough capacity to meet both AI and non-AI, or is there a part of your strategy where you intend to wind down some of the non-AI portion of your capacity to allocate more towards AI?

We do both. Usually we don't like to see 95% or 100% utilization, because this gave us no room. Now because the demand grows too fast, so in theory, if the capacity, I mean the utilization can be like 85 to 90%, this can be very, very healthy. And we are targeting that kind of goal.

Got it. And if I may ask, based on that capacity plan and utilization rate, that sort of implies that unless there is a price hike in Q1, Q1 revenues will be relatively flat on a sequential basis before we start to see revenues grow again in Q2 onwards driven by that new capacity coming online. Is that kind of the right way to think about your top-line momentum?

For the time being, I think we can only give you the Q4 guidance. So when the quarter is getting closer, then we can give you a more clear picture about the Q1 revenue guidance. But again, from the demand side, we still very strong BB ratio, and we are working on everything to have the extra capacity to fulfill that.
Got it. Thank you. Is there any CapEx guidance for this year and next year that can be shared with us?

We've spent about 5.7 billion NT dollars this year up to September end. Quarter 4 may slow down a little bit on that run rate, but all in all, I think this year has been growing versus last year. Next year, there's some plan in there, but I don't have guidance for 2027 yet.

Got it. Thank you, Eddie. And in terms of raw material for tantalum especially, I think there's a lot of questions that we received from investors around this. Is this something that concerns you or is it something that is a risk going into next year?

Well, actually we've been doing a lot of efforts on that front. First, the tantalum powder price has been stabilized since early this year, so we don't see the same dynamic that we observed last year. Second, we're doing a lot of strategic buying actually since early this year that sort of contribute to our inventory this year, although still very healthy. I think at this moment, we're looking at 115 days inventory turnover, better than before, but this already include those strategic buy we did for tantalum. So at this moment, we don't see any major issues for next year on tantalum powder.

And one more remark is especially we have good understanding with the customer. Because the cost increased in past, that was a fact. So we did pass this kind of cost increase to customer to reflect in our selling price. That's why you see although the cost is increased, we can always maintain steadily growing gross margin.

I see. And so it's fair to assume that when you think about pricing and how you price your product to your end customer, it's not based on how much you intend to make based on your services, but more from what kind of gross margin you intend to make? Not from an absolute dollar perspective, but more from a percentage perspective. Is that the right way to think about it?

Certainly, Howard. I think any company is trying to preserve the healthiness of the of the business. I think this is a general philosophy. Now for us in particular, we try to do so because take tantalum as an example, it requires massive investment in CapEx, in R&D, also, you know, inventory. As Gaven said, there is an investment that Yageo did through KEMET before the acquisition. About 100 million dollar was invested in the supply chain and vertical integration of tantalum by KEMET 15 or so years ago. And at that time for KEMET, 100 million dollar was a very big number.

And so when you think about that framework, then obviously in order to be the supplier that is reliable, that is present, that can support demand for a long period of time, then you need to be able to maintain or always look for ways to stay healthy margin-wise. So when a cost like that impacts you, you got to have conversation with your customer, because you still need that margin to really be reinvested in the business. Obviously each case is different, each customer is different, but as a philosophy, this is what we try to do. We try not to be opportunistic, we try to stay vigilant, to stay healthy. And sometimes you need to also accept and be subject to the rules of supply and demand when there are extremes. But in general, that's the philosophy that we apply in our pricing conversations with customers.

And so far, I've seen and I perceived that it's been very well understood and went very well. We try to give predictability and fairness and openness and transparency whenever we can. And whatever we do is not to auction that capacity for a month or two, is to commit to that customer for a long period of time to the supply that he is trying to secure. So very fair conversation, and in the end, both parties are always happy to reach that agreement.

Got it. Thank you. That's good to hear, because within my coverage there are some companies like the ODMs who are not able to price based on a percentage of margin, but more from an absolute dollar perspective. So there are definitely companies that want to do that, but unfortunately are not able to, so that's good to hear. But just coming back to your conversations with customers on capacity and supply over the next couple of years, we've seen across many different subsegments where customers are willing to book a entire production site or subsidize on CapEx. Is this something that is also happening within the passive component space from what you're seeing?

Yeah, we had... I would start by saying we have experience with several type of agreements. We, meaning Yageo Group, in its collection of different acquisition over the past 20 years, we experience examples where customers helped to fund the CapEx and they got that capital back over a period of time as they consume product. And in that case, obviously part of the agreement was to reserve that extra capacity for them. We had cases where, and we also made this public through a press release, we co-invested with a large customer of ours to open a new factory in a new country, in India. And that was the result of a desire from that customer to have a supplier that have that footprint, and that led to a co-investment.

We had example where sometimes the CapEx is not shared, but there are commitments on the orders and the cancellation terms and conditions of those orders, that we can secure our return. There is all sort of formulas. We had it all. And we are open to discuss all of this with customers, depending on what fits for them. What we will not do, however, is to basically sell out a significant portion of our capacity to just a handful of customers that might even opportunistically try to secure and buy out, or even worse, just store the product, and therefore damaging everything else and everybody else. This we try not to do. We always try to make sure that whatever we do, we can carry all our customer base, which is more than 270,000 when you look at distribution POS, try to carry all of them forward and make sure we don't just leave them behind.

In the past, we had to also sometimes refuse a couple of ask that were trying to secure and speculate on some of the products that we had, tantalum in particular. And so we are very aware of that, and being the number one supplier of tantalum polymer in particular in the world, we have a duty to our customers and we take that seriously.
Got it. Thank you so much. And I think that is the last question that we have. Maybe I'll pass it back to you, David, to see if you have any closing remarks.

Thank you, Howard, and thank you, all the investors. I think this year we can expect a very, very strong closing for the 2026, maybe in both top line and bottom line. Maybe this will be the one of historical record in Yageo, in Yageo Group. And certainly we appreciate the opportunity brought by AI. But for management side, we know we don't take this for granted. We are still very careful in the price management, cost control, and the efficiency improvement. And hopefully in next earnings call, we can share more good news with you. Thank you.

Thank you. And with that, we'll bring today's webcast to a close. On behalf of Morgan Stanley, I'd like to thank David, Eddie, Claudio, and Gaven for their time and for sharing their perspectives on the results and outlook. Thank you to everyone as well who joined us today for your interest and participation. We look forward to welcoming you back for our next webcast. Thank you, and see you all next time.
Thank you, Howard. Thank you, all.
Thank you.
